solutions.text: Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Oil is a finite resource that will eventually run out if we keep using it at this rate. — FINITE (adj) = hữu hạn, có giới hạn; collocation "a finite resource/finite reserves". Lưu ý phân biệt với "infinite" (vô hạn).

2. Solar and wind power are often intermittent, since they only work under certain weather conditions. — INTERMITTENT (adj) = gián đoạn, không liên tục; collocation "intermittent supply/renewables/output".
3. Many countries are trying to increase their use of renewable energy, such as sunlight and wind. — RENEWABLE (adj) = tái tạo, không cạn kiệt; collocation "renewable energy/resources/transition".

4. Engineers are finding new ways to harness solar power and turn it into electricity. — HARNESS (v) = khai thác, tận dụng (nguồn năng lượng tự nhiên); collocation "harness solar power/the wind/geothermal energy".

5. Radioactive waste from nuclear power plants must be stored very carefully because it remains dangerous for centuries. — RADIOACTIVE (adj) = có tính phóng xạ; collocation "radioactive waste/material", "highly radioactive".
6. Iceland generates a large share of its electricity from geothermal energy. — GEOTHERMAL (adj) = địa nhiệt; collocation "geothermal energy/power", "harness geothermal energy".

7. The combustion of fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, which is one of the main causes of climate change. — COMBUSTION (n) = sự đốt cháy; collocation "combustion of fossil fuels", "internal combustion engine".
8. Households that reduce their energy consumption each month can significantly cut their bills. — CONSUMPTION (n) = mức tiêu thụ; collocation "curb/reduce energy consumption", "high consumption".

9. Experts argue that keeping the national grid stable is one of the biggest challenges of the energy transition. — GRID (n) = lưới điện; collocation "the national grid", "grid stability", "feed into the grid".

10. Several old coal-fired power stations will be decommissioned over the next decade. — DECOMMISSION (v) = ngừng hoạt động và tháo dỡ (nhà máy, lò phản ứng); collocation "decommission coal plants/a reactor".

11. Some rural communities in Vietnam are now energy self-sufficient thanks to solar power. — SELF-SUFFICIENT (adj) = tự cung tự cấp; collocation "energy self-sufficient", "self-sufficient household", "become self-sufficient".

12. Governments across the world are grappling with the difficult question of how to replace coal without raising prices. — GRAPPLE WITH (phrasal v) = vật lộn, cố gắng giải quyết (vấn đề khó); collocation "grapple with a challenge/an issue/the problem".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: As solar panels become more affordable, an increasing number of households are choosing to install them. Band 8: With the cost of photovoltaic panels falling sharply, homeowners are increasingly drawn to rooftop solar as a means of cutting long-term electricity bills.

2. Band 7: Nuclear power remains controversial, largely because of public concerns about accidents and radioactive waste. Band 8: Despite its potential as a low-carbon baseload source, nuclear power continues to provoke controversy, chiefly owing to lingering public anxiety over safety and long-term waste disposal.

3. Band 7: Governments should provide greater financial support for renewable energy projects. Band 8: Were governments to channel more substantial subsidies into renewable energy projects, the transition away from fossil fuels would almost certainly accelerate.

4. Band 7: Wind power cannot always be depended upon, since wind speeds fluctuate throughout the day. Band 8: Because wind speeds fluctuate unpredictably, wind power remains an inherently intermittent source that grids must supplement with more dispatchable alternatives.

5. Band 7: Low-income families often spend a disproportionately large share of their income on energy bills. Band 8: It is low-income households that typically bear the heaviest burden, devoting a disproportionate share of their earnings to electricity and heating costs.

6. Band 7: Coal-fired power stations generate significant pollution and are gradually being phased out. Band 8: Owing to the substantial pollution they generate, coal-fired power stations are steadily being phased out in favour of cleaner alternatives.

7. Band 7: Countries that rely too heavily on imported oil and gas can be severely affected by fluctuating prices. Band 8: Nations overly dependent on imported fossil fuels find themselves acutely vulnerable to price volatility, a risk that domestic renewable capacity could substantially mitigate.

8. Band 7: Conserving energy at home can benefit both the environment and household finances. Band 8: Far from being a purely environmental gesture, conserving energy at home also yields tangible financial benefits, easing pressure on household budgets over time.

passages.text: Among engineers working on the decarbonisation of electricity grids, two technologies have come to dominate the long-term planning conversation: green hydrogen produced by electrolysis, and grid-scale lithium-ion batteries paired with utility solar and wind. The two are sometimes presented as complementary, sometimes as rivals, and the relative weight assigned to each carries substantial implications for industrial policy. Recent research has begun to clarify where each technology performs well, where each performs poorly, and where the underlying economics remain too unsettled to support confident projections.

The technical case for green hydrogen rests on its energy density and its capacity for long-duration storage. Unlike a lithium battery, which discharges over hours, hydrogen produced in summer can in principle be retained until winter, when solar generation falls. Professor Annika Lindqvist, an electrochemical engineer at Chalmers University of Technology in Gothenburg, has argued that this seasonal-storage capability gives hydrogen an irreplaceable role in grids with high winter demand. Her group's modelling suggests that, even under optimistic battery cost trajectories, regions north of the fiftieth parallel cannot achieve full decarbonisation without a substantial hydrogen component. Lindqvist concedes that current electrolyser efficiency remains modest, with round-trip losses of around 65 per cent once reconversion to electricity is accounted for, but she expects incremental improvements to narrow this gap.

A markedly different reading is offered by Dr Hiroshi Tanaka, a power systems researcher at Kyoto University. Tanaka's group has compared the levelised cost of stored energy across a range of jurisdictions and concluded that hydrogen is competitive only in a relatively narrow set of use cases, notably steel production, ammonia synthesis and heavy long-haul transport. For routine grid balancing on diurnal timescales, Tanaka argues, lithium-ion batteries paired with modest demand-side flexibility consistently outperform hydrogen on cost, efficiency and deployment speed. He stresses that this finding does not amount to an argument against hydrogen as such, only against the prevailing assumption in some policy documents that hydrogen should be expected to displace batteries across the entire grid.

The capital cost trajectory of grid-scale batteries has lent considerable weight to Tanaka's reading. According to data compiled by the United States National Renewable Energy Laboratory, installed costs for utility lithium-ion systems fell from approximately 700 dollars per kilowatt-hour in 2015 to roughly 270 dollars per kilowatt-hour in 2024, a decline that has consistently outpaced expert forecasts. Dr Esperanza Morales, a materials scientist affiliated with Sandia National Laboratories, has documented parallel improvements in cell chemistry, particularly lithium-iron-phosphate variants that exhibit longer cycle life and lower fire risk. Morales has cautioned, however, that current cost declines will probably moderate over the coming decade as the technology matures and as raw-material constraints on lithium and nickel begin to bind more visibly.

A further consideration concerns sourcing and supply chains. Hydrogen, in its green form, requires substantial freshwater inputs and very large quantities of zero-carbon electricity. Critics have observed that producing one kilogram of green hydrogen consumes approximately nine litres of fresh water and around fifty kilowatt-hours of electricity, an aggregate that scales poorly under drought conditions. Lithium batteries, by contrast, present concentrated extraction impacts at the mining stage but minimal operational resource demand once installed. Whether the diffuse, ongoing footprint of hydrogen or the front-loaded footprint of batteries imposes a heavier overall burden is a question on which the research literature has not converged.

The policy implications of these competing readings have grown increasingly contentious. Industrial planners in Germany, Japan and South Korea have committed substantial public funds to hydrogen infrastructure, partly on the reasoning advanced by Lindqvist that no purely battery-based pathway is viable in temperate northern grids. Others, including several analysts at the International Energy Agency, have argued that public subsidy should be concentrated on the so-called hard-to-abate sectors that Tanaka identifies, leaving routine grid balancing to batteries. Dr Faisal Al-Mansoori, an energy economist at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology, has proposed an intermediate position: hydrogen production should be co-located with renewable generation in regions of seasonal surplus, with batteries handling shorter timescales. Al-Mansoori notes that this division of labour has yet to be tested at scale, and that institutional inertia in legacy gas networks may complicate its adoption.

What the three positions appear to share is a recognition that the dichotomy between hydrogen and batteries is, on closer inspection, less stark than early advocacy on either side implied. Hydrogen retains a defensible role in seasonal storage and in industries that lithium chemistry cannot easily decarbonise. Batteries retain a defensible role in diurnal balancing, where their efficiency and rapid deployability are difficult to match. The contested terrain lies in the middle range — storage events of several days to several weeks — and it is here, the writer suggests, that genuine technological competition is most likely to determine deployment in the coming decade. Whether public policy can hold open this competitive space, rather than committing prematurely to a single dominant architecture, may matter more for eventual grid decarbonisation than any further marginal improvement in either technology on its own.

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture closes our materials-recovery unit — moving from rare-earth magnets to the much more politicised and, frankly, more economically pressing question of recovering lithium from spent batteries. [pause:5s] The conceptual armature I'll deploy is drawn from the work of Professor Wenshu Yagoda — that's Y-A-G-O-D-A, no umlaut, no double-G. Yagoda's 2018 patent series restructured industrial recovery thought, replacing the older pyrometallurgical defaults with what she terms "selective hydrometallurgical cascade theory". [pause:3s] First, some historical orientation. The pilot recovery plant whose throughput figures I'll quote was commissioned in 2014 — sorry, let me correct that, 2012; the audited yield data published in 2014 covered operating runs that began in 2012. So whenever I reference the commissioning year, please record 2012. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation. Yagoda's cascade USED TO be evaluated only by gross recovered tonnage — quite a blunt metric — NOW the field benchmarks by purity-grade-weighted yield, and from 2029 a European consortium WILL be rolling out closed-loop direct-recycling reactors that bypass the leach step entirely. So past, present, future. For today's session I'm focusing on the CURRENT benchmarking regime — that is, the purity-grade-weighted approach. Moving to terminology. The recovery pathway Yagoda foregrounds — selectively dissolving the cathode active material in mild acid before separating the value metals — is termed "wet leaching". Now, you'll see related labels in the legacy chemical-engineering literature: solvent extraction, aqueous digestion, acid bleed recovery. All gesture toward overlapping operations, but they are NOT interchangeable with Yagoda's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is wet leaching — w-e-t l-e-a-c-h-i-n-g. So when the legacy corpus uses solvent extraction or aqueous digestion, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to flag is what process chemists call the "purity-grade cascade". When metallurgists describe how recovered lithium graduates from low-spec industrial salt up to battery-grade carbonate, they sketch a graded cascade running from technical grade through fertilizer grade to battery grade to electronic grade. So, you know, you'll find a kilogram of technical-grade lithium carbonate selling for a fraction of the battery-grade equivalent — that's the price spread we exploit. Or producers blending two grades to hit a contract spec mid-supply — that's grade-blending arbitrage. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical label. The umbrella term is the purity-grade cascade. [pause:3s] Now, the throughput data — and please pay close attention because the quantifiers cluster densely here. Of the eight hundred and forty tonnes of black-mass feedstock we processed across five pilot lines last fiscal year, MOST yielded battery-grade lithium carbonate — roughly seventy-four per cent. Only a few tonnes — about eleven per cent — were downgraded to technical grade after off-spec sampling, and some — fifteen per cent — were lost as process residue. So battery-grade dominates numerically, but the residue tail, though small, is environmentally significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to introduce is "electrolyte regeneration". This refers to the temporal process by which the spent electrolyte fluid is purified and re-deployed within the same recovery loop, rather than incinerated. At the Trondheim pilot, our team logged sixty-two completed regeneration cycles across one operating quarter. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that pyrometallurgical smelting outperforms hydrometallurgy on net carbon footprint is, frankly, not supported. Most of the lifecycle assays in our dataset did NOT show the predicted monotonic emissions advantage for smelting over wet leaching. Quite the opposite — many showed an inverted curve, with smelting performing worst when the cobalt fraction was low. So the older "smelt-is-cleaner" hypothesis, which predicts uniform emissions gains, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I opened with. That CURRENT purity-grade-weighted state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in next Tuesday's seminar. I want you to focus on the purity-grade weighting protocols specifically, not the closed-loop reactor futures or the legacy tonnage instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: lithium recovery operates as a selective cascade, not a single-pass smelt; the technical term for mild-acid cathode dissolution is wet leaching; battery-grade yield dominates pilot output at roughly seventy-four per cent; and the smelt-is-cleaner hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'll move to cobalt-stream recovery. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The diagram outlines the eight-stage process by which solar radiation is captured at a photovoltaic farm and ultimately distributed to consumers via the national grid.

Overall, the process can be divided into two broad phases: on-site generation and conditioning, followed by transmission and distribution. A key feature is the integration of a storage bank, which compensates for the otherwise intermittent supply typical of solar power.

Initially, sunlight is absorbed by silicon panels, where it is converted into low-voltage DC electricity. The output of several panel strings is then aggregated in a combiner box before being fed into an inverter that transforms direct current into alternating current. Following this, a step-up transformer raises the voltage to 33 kilovolts. Any surplus is routed to lithium-ion batteries to support dispatchable generation and maintain grid stability.

Subsequently, a substation boosts the voltage further to 230 kilovolts, allowing the cleaned-up energy to be transmitted across long distances. Finally, the electricity reaches homes, factories and EV chargers via the national grid, thereby accelerating the broader renewable transition away from fossil fuels.
The diagram delineates the eight discrete stages through which sunlight is harnessed at a photovoltaic farm and ultimately conveyed to consumers across the national grid.

Overall, what stands out is the two-phase structure of the operation: an initial sequence of on-site generation and electrical conditioning precedes a transmission phase that carries power over long distances. Equally notable is the diversion of surplus output to a storage bank, a feature that buffers the inherently intermittent nature of solar generation.

Initially, photons striking the silicon panels are converted into low-voltage direct current, the output of numerous strings being aggregated in a combiner box. This current is then fed into an inverter, where it is transformed into alternating current, before a step-up transformer elevates the voltage to 33 kilovolts. At this point, any excess is diverted to lithium-ion cells to enable dispatchable generation.

Thereafter, a substation raises the voltage still further, to 230 kilovolts, so that the power can be transmitted efficiently over distance. Only at the final stage does the electricity reach homes, factories and EV chargers, thereby reinforcing the wider transition toward renewable energy.

Encouraging households and businesses to go green through efficiency upgrades, such as better insulation and LED lighting, can meaningfully curb overall consumption.
Many environmentalists firmly believe that an immediate, wholesale switch to renewable energy is the only responsible path given the finite window to avert catastrophic warming.
Sceptics argue that abandoning dispatchable fossil-fuel plants too quickly, before storage technology matures, would jeopardise energy security.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The proposal to scale up nuclear power as a remedy for the climate emergency has gained renewed traction among policymakers. While the technology is not without its hazards, I largely agree that a measured expansion is justified, provided strict safeguards are in place.

The strongest argument in favour of nuclear lies in its energy density and reliability. Unlike wind and solar — which remain intermittent and require costly storage — a single reactor can supply gigawatts of low-carbon baseload power around the clock. The International Energy Agency has noted that countries which retired their nuclear fleets prematurely, such as Germany, ended up burning more coal during the transition. It is precisely this dispatchable nature of nuclear that makes it a useful complement to renewables rather than a competitor.

That said, the objections are far from trivial. Reactor meltdowns at Chernobyl and Fukushima have demonstrated how a single accident can render vast tracts of land uninhabitable for generations. Furthermore, the safe storage of high-level radioactive waste remains an unresolved engineering problem, with most spent fuel still sitting in cooling pools awaiting a permanent repository. The capital costs and build times of new reactors are also notoriously prohibitive, often running into tens of billions and decades.

In my opinion, these risks justify caution but not outright rejection. New Generation IV designs, including small modular reactors, are inherently safer and produce less long-lived waste. Pairing such reactors with an expanding share of renewables would diversify the grid and accelerate the phase-out of coal.

In conclusion, although the perils of nuclear power should not be downplayed, its capacity to deliver clean baseload electricity is too valuable to discard, and a carefully regulated expansion appears to be the pragmatic path forward.

The contention that a global build-out of nuclear capacity is indispensable to climate stabilisation has resurfaced with surprising vigour. While I do not endorse it without reservation, I broadly concur that a disciplined expansion — anchored in next-generation designs and rigorous oversight — represents one of the most pragmatic levers available.

A compelling rationale for nuclear lies in its near-zero operational carbon footprint coupled with a power density unmatched by any renewable. Whereas a sprawling solar farm may yield only a few hundred megawatts contingent on insolation, a single large reactor delivers a steady gigawatt regardless of meteorological vagaries. The International Energy Agency's Net Zero roadmap accordingly envisages a doubling of installed nuclear capacity, recognising that decarbonising electricity grids without firm low-carbon generation is mathematically improbable. Especially in regions lacking geothermal or hydroelectric endowment, nuclear may be the only dispatchable substitute for fossil-fired plants.

Detractors, nevertheless, marshal arguments that cannot be dismissed lightly. The legacy of Fukushima continues to haunt public opinion, and the geological disposal of high-level waste remains technically feasible yet politically intractable. Equally troubling are the astronomical capital expenditures and build timelines of conventional reactors, which routinely overrun by a decade. Were these vulnerabilities ignored, a hasty roll-out could trigger backlash and stall the broader energy transition.

The resolution, in my view, lies in selective rather than indiscriminate deployment. Small modular reactors — factory-built, passively safe and an order of magnitude cheaper — promise to mitigate many of these structural drawbacks. Embedding them within a grid increasingly dominated by renewables would yield a hybrid system both resilient and decarbonised.

To sum up, although nuclear power is no panacea and its risks merit sober scrutiny, abandoning it would substantially impair humanity's chances of meeting mid-century climate targets, making prudent expansion the wiser course.

B. CUE CARD + MODEL ANSWER
Cue Card:
Describe an energy-saving practice in your home or country.
You should say:
what the practice is
when and how it is carried out
who is involved
and explain why this practice matters.
Model Answer (265 words):

The energy-saving practice I'd like to highlight is my family's adoption of a comprehensive household efficiency regime, anchored by a rooftop photovoltaic system we installed three years ago and a meticulous appliance-management routine that's become second nature to us all.

The way it operates is genuinely systematic. Our 5-kilowatt solar array, mounted on the south-facing roof, generates the bulk of our daytime electricity needs - powering everything from the air conditioner to the rice cooker - while a smart inverter feeds surplus output back into the national grid. Beyond generation, we've replaced every incandescent bulb with LEDs, retrofitted the apartment with thermal-insulating curtains, and programmed a smart thermostat to optimise cooling cycles around our occupancy patterns.

Every household member is actively involved. My father monitors the solar app obsessively, my mother schedules the washing machine to run during peak generation hours, and even my younger siblings have internalised the habit of unplugging chargers - vampire loads being the bane of his existence, as my father puts it.

What makes this practice genuinely consequential, in my view, transcends the mere financial savings, considerable though they are. Vietnam's energy grid remains predominantly coal-dependent, and every kilowatt-hour we self-generate is a kilowatt-hour that needn't be produced through fossil-fuel combustion. Moreover, the practice has fostered an ambient energy-consciousness in our home that gradually permeates other decisions: how we commute, what appliances we purchase, even what we eat.
In short, this isn't just thrift - it's a modest but tangible contribution to the broader energy transition, one rooftop at a time.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The Intermittency Problem: Wind and solar power cannot generate electricity 24/7. This requires massive advancements in "Energy Storage Solutions" (like lithium-ion mega-batteries) to keep the grid stable.

The Nuclear Debate: Nuclear energy produces zero carbon emissions and provides a massive, reliable baseload. However, disasters like Chernobyl and Fukushima, along with the issue of radioactive waste, make it highly controversial.
Net-Zero by 2050: Many developed nations have pledged to become carbon-neutral by 2050, requiring a massive paradigm shift from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to Electric Vehicles (EVs).
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Immediate Switch to Renewable Energy vs. Gradual Transition

For Immediate Switch: Climate change has reached a catastrophic tipping point; fossil fuels are finite and cause irreversible environmental damage; heavy investment now will make renewables cheaper in the long run.

For Gradual Transition (Pros of Fossil Fuels currently): The current grid infrastructure cannot handle intermittent renewable energy yet; an immediate ban on fossil fuels would cause a global economic collapse and astronomical energy prices; developing nations rely on cheap coal to lift their citizens out of poverty.
Topic: Nuclear Energy (Is it the best solution?)

Arguments FOR (Pros): Exceptionally high energy density; produces no greenhouse gas emissions during operation; unlike solar/wind, it provides a constant, reliable baseload of power unaffected by weather.

Arguments AGAINST (Cons): The catastrophic risk of reactor meltdowns; the unresolved problem of storing highly radioactive waste for millennia; astronomical construction costs and long build times compared to wind/solar farms.
Topic: Individual Responsibility vs. Government Action in Energy Conservation
Government: Can implement carbon taxes, subsidise green technology, and fund massive infrastructure projects like national grids and public transport.

Individuals: Can adopt sustainable habits (using public transport, insulating homes to reduce heating consumption, avoiding single-use plastics); individual consumer demand drives companies to "go green".

Model Answer (265 words):

The energy-saving practice I'd like to highlight is my family's adoption of a comprehensive household efficiency regime, anchored by a rooftop photovoltaic system we installed three years ago and a meticulous appliance-management routine that's become second nature to us all.

The way it operates is genuinely systematic. Our 5-kilowatt solar array, mounted on the south-facing roof, generates the bulk of our daytime electricity needs - powering everything from the air conditioner to the rice cooker - while a smart inverter feeds surplus output back into the national grid. Beyond generation, we've replaced every incandescent bulb with LEDs, retrofitted the apartment with thermal-insulating curtains, and programmed a smart thermostat to optimise cooling cycles around our occupancy patterns.

Every household member is actively involved. My father monitors the solar app obsessively, my mother schedules the washing machine to run during peak generation hours, and even my younger siblings have internalised the habit of unplugging chargers - vampire loads being the bane of his existence, as my father puts it.

What makes this practice genuinely consequential, in my view, transcends the mere financial savings, considerable though they are. Vietnam's energy grid remains predominantly coal-dependent, and every kilowatt-hour we self-generate is a kilowatt-hour that needn't be produced through fossil-fuel combustion. Moreover, the practice has fostered an ambient energy-consciousness in our home that gradually permeates other decisions: how we commute, what appliances we purchase, even what we eat.
In short, this isn't just thrift - it's a modest but tangible contribution to the broader energy transition, one rooftop at a time.
Q1: Should governments subsidise renewable energy more aggressively?

P (Point): Substantial government subsidisation of renewables is, I believe, not merely justified but economically rational, particularly when one accounts for the externalised costs of fossil-fuel dependency.

E (Explain): The argument that renewables should "compete on a level playing field" rings hollow when fossil fuels have enjoyed over a century of explicit and implicit subsidies, including tax breaks, infrastructure underwriting, and unpriced pollution externalities.

E (Evidence): An IMF working paper (Parry et al., 2021) calculated that global fossil-fuel subsidies - including unpriced environmental and health costs - amounted to a staggering 5.9 trillion USD in 2020, equivalent to roughly 6.8% of global GDP. Meanwhile, IRENA's Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2022 report documented that the levelised cost of solar PV has fallen 89% since 2010, demonstrating that targeted subsidies catalyse rapid cost reductions through economies of scale.

L (Link): Consequently, rather than questioning whether to subsidise renewables, the genuine debate should centre on how rapidly fossil-fuel subsidies can be phased out and redirected to accelerate the energy transition.
Q2: Is nuclear power safe enough to be a major part of the future energy mix?

P (Point): While public perception of nuclear power remains coloured by historic disasters, the empirical safety record - especially of modern Generation III and IV reactor designs - suggests that nuclear deserves serious reconsideration as a dispatchable low-carbon baseload source.

E (Explain): The fundamental dilemma is that variable renewables, despite their virtues, cannot yet provide the round-the-clock dispatchable power that modern grids require, leaving a gap that gas and coal currently fill - with catastrophic climate consequences.

E (Evidence): A landmark analysis in Environmental Science & Technology (Kharecha & Hansen, 2013) estimated that nuclear power had prevented approximately 1.84 million air-pollution-related deaths globally between 1971 and 2009, far outweighing fatalities from nuclear incidents. More recently, Our World in Data (Ritchie, 2020) calculated nuclear's mortality rate per terawatt-hour at 0.03 deaths, comparable to wind (0.04) and dramatically lower than coal (24.6).
L (Link): Therefore, while waste management and proliferation concerns warrant rigorous oversight, dismissing nuclear outright may well constitute a strategic error in the race to decarbonise.
Q3: Will energy poverty worsen in the coming decades?

P (Point): Energy poverty risks deepening considerably in the coming decades unless deliberate policy intervention is undertaken, although the trajectory is not predetermined and remains highly responsive to deliberate political choices.

E (Explain): The combination of climate-driven price volatility, the unequal costs of the energy transition, and geopolitical disruptions to fossil-fuel markets disproportionately burdens low-income households, who already spend a significantly higher share of income on energy.

E (Evidence): The IEA's World Energy Outlook 2023 warned that approximately 745 million people globally still lacked access to electricity in 2022 - a figure that actually rose for the first time in a decade due to the post-pandemic energy crisis. Furthermore, a study in Nature Energy (Bednar et al., 2020) found that in the United States alone, low-income households face energy burdens three times higher than their wealthier counterparts.

L (Link): What this underscores is the urgency of embedding equity considerations into climate policy - through measures like progressive carbon dividends and targeted retrofit subsidies - to ensure the energy transition is genuinely just rather than merely green.

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas

Grid stability issues arising from solar and wind intermittency will be central.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Right, picking up where we left off — the so-called energy transition. The framing is seductive: renewables get cheaper, fossil fuels retreat, emissions fall. I want to complicate this picture in three ways. The reality is messier, slower, and more politically contested than the press releases concede.

> First, grid stability. A modern electricity grid must balance supply and demand on a sub-second basis. Coal and gas plants offer dispatchable power; solar and wind, by contrast, are intermittent — output rises and falls with weather and time of day. As variable renewables approach roughly forty percent of supply, system operators encounter what engineers call the duck curve: a deep midday solar trough followed by a fierce evening ramp. Battery storage helps, but utility-scale storage at the terawatt-hour level remains, frankly, in its infancy.

> Second, the political economy. Decarbonisation is not a technical problem; it is a stranded-asset problem. Trillions of dollars of coal mines, refineries and pipelines must be written off, and the communities dependent on them require what policymakers euphemistically call a "just transition" — retraining, regional investment, wage replacement. Without it, the transition will stall on the ballot box.

> Third — and this is the conceptual sting — the Jevons paradox, identified by the economist William Stanley Jevons in 1865. He observed that as steam engines became more efficient, total coal consumption rose rather than fell, because cheaper energy spawned new uses. We see the modern echo: LED lighting is ten times more efficient than incandescent, yet global lighting energy use keeps climbing. Efficiency, on its own, is not enough.

Now, having laid out those three complications, I want to spend a few minutes on something the textbooks gloss over entirely — the materials bottleneck. Because here is the awkward truth: a decarbonised economy is not a dematerialised one. It is, if anything, more mineral-hungry. The International Energy Agency has modelled that an electric vehicle requires roughly six times the mineral input of a conventional car — copper, lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite. [pause] Scale that across an entire vehicle fleet, plus the grid storage and the transmission build-out, and you confront a demand curve for these metals that the current mining pipeline simply cannot meet on the timeline politicians promise.

And mines, well, mines are slow. The lead time from discovery to first production now averages something like sixteen years. You cannot legislate a copper deposit into existence by 2030. So we inherit a fresh dependency — one that is geographically concentrated in uncomfortable ways. The Democratic Republic of Congo supplies the lion's share of cobalt; refining capacity for many critical minerals sits overwhelmingly in a single jurisdiction. We have, in a sense, traded an oil cartel for a minerals chokepoint.

Let me press the contradiction further. There is a temporal mismatch nobody likes to name. Building all this clean infrastructure — the turbines, the panels, the batteries — is itself enormously carbon-intensive up front. You spend emissions today to save emissions tomorrow. The payback is real, but it means our near-term emissions curve may bulge before it bends. [pause] Um, that is politically toxic, because voters experience the cost now and the benefit later.

This is where the circular economy enters — recycling, urban mining, designing batteries for recovery rather than disposal. A second-life battery is, after all, a domestic mineral reserve. So the question that ought to frame everything we decide next is whether supply-side ambition can ever outrun these physical and geological constraints, or whether…
> The take-home is uncomfortable. Without demand-side restraint, we may decarbonise the grid only to rebound elsewhere. Now, turning to figure two…

T12 — ENERGY & RESOURCES · Writing Task 1 (Process diagram (solar farm to national grid, eight stages))
(a) Đề bài & biểu đồ / số liệu

Đề bài.  The diagram below illustrates how electricity is generated at a solar farm and delivered to the national grid, in eight stages. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
Quy trình (Process diagram (solar farm to national grid, eight stages)).

rows: Sunlight strikes silicon panels arranged across the solar farm.
The panels convert photons into low-voltage direct-current (DC) electricity.
The output of several panel strings is aggregated in a combiner box.
The direct current is converted into alternating current (AC) by an inverter.
A transformer raises the AC voltage from 480 V to 33 kV.
Any surplus output is diverted to lithium-ion cells for later use.
Voltage is stepped up again to 230 kV for long-distance transmission.
Electricity reaches homes, factories and EV chargers via the grid.

blocks.text: (b) Từ vựng mô tả số liệu (Band 8 data-description)

rows: The process opens with photovoltaic capture, as sunlight strikes the silicon panels.
The panels convert photons into low-voltage direct-current electricity.
The output of several strings is aggregated before being fed into the inverter.
A transformer steps up the voltage from 480 volts to 33 kilovolts.
Any surplus output is diverted to lithium-ion cells for storage.
Battery storage enables dispatchable generation and maintains grid stability.

blocks.text: (c) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Overview · Body 1 · Body 2
•  Introduction — paraphrase the diagram as an eight-stage process turning sunlight into grid electricity for consumers.
•  Overview — note two broad phases (on-site generation and conditioning, then transmission and distribution) and the integration of battery storage; no specific stages or voltages.
•  Body 1 — describe Stages 1–4: photovoltaic capture, DC generation, aggregation in the combiner box, and DC-to-AC inversion.
•  Body 2 — describe Stages 5–8: step-up to 33 kV, diversion of surplus to batteries, substation boost to 230 kV, and distribution across the national grid.
(d) Mẫu câu luyện tập (Practice sentences)

rows: Mở bài diễn giải quy trình tám bước
The diagram outlines the eight-stage process by which solar radiation is captured at a photovoltaic farm and ultimately distributed via the national grid.
Dùng 'by which ... is captured ... distributed' cho register kỹ thuật.
Câu Overview chia hai pha (không số liệu)
Overall, the process falls into two broad phases — on-site generation and conditioning, followed by long-distance transmission — with a storage bank buffering the intermittent supply.
Overview KHÔNG nêu mức điện áp cụ thể.
Mô tả chuyển đổi DC sang AC bằng bị động
The output of several panel strings is then aggregated in a combiner box before being fed into an inverter that transforms DC into AC.
Chuỗi bị động 'is aggregated ... being fed into'.
Mô tả lưu trữ và truyền tải
Any surplus is routed to lithium-ion batteries to support dispatchable generation, after which a substation boosts the voltage for transmission.
Dùng 'after which' để nối khâu lưu trữ và truyền tải.

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~175 từ)
The diagram outlines the eight-stage process by which solar radiation is captured at a photovoltaic farm and ultimately distributed to consumers via the national grid.

Overall, the process can be divided into two broad phases: on-site generation and conditioning, followed by transmission and distribution. A key feature is the integration of a storage bank, which compensates for the otherwise intermittent supply typical of solar power.

Initially, sunlight is absorbed by silicon panels, where it is converted into low-voltage DC electricity. The output of several panel strings is then aggregated in a combiner box before being fed into an inverter that transforms direct current into alternating current. Following this, a step-up transformer raises the voltage to 33 kilovolts. Any surplus is routed to lithium-ion batteries to support dispatchable generation and maintain grid stability.

Subsequently, a substation boosts the voltage further to 230 kilovolts, allowing the cleaned-up energy to be transmitted across long distances. Finally, the electricity reaches homes, factories and EV chargers via the national grid, thereby accelerating the broader renewable transition away from fossil fuels.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~183 từ)
The diagram delineates the eight discrete stages through which sunlight is harnessed at a photovoltaic farm and ultimately conveyed to consumers across the national grid.

Overall, what stands out is the two-phase structure of the operation: an initial sequence of on-site generation and electrical conditioning precedes a transmission phase that carries power over long distances. Equally notable is the diversion of surplus output to a storage bank, a feature that buffers the inherently intermittent nature of solar generation.

Initially, photons striking the silicon panels are converted into low-voltage direct current, the output of numerous strings being aggregated in a combiner box. This current is then fed into an inverter, where it is transformed into alternating current, before a step-up transformer elevates the voltage to 33 kilovolts. At this point, any excess is diverted to lithium-ion cells to enable dispatchable generation.

Thereafter, a substation raises the voltage still further, to 230 kilovolts, so that the power can be transmitted efficiently over distance. Only at the final stage does the electricity reach homes, factories and EV chargers, thereby reinforcing the wider transition toward renewable energy.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 mở Overview bằng nhận định cấu trúc ('two-phase structure', 'diversion of surplus ... buffers the intermittent nature') thay vì chỉ liệt kê hai pha như Band 7, thể hiện Task Achievement cao hơn.

•  Band 8 dùng đảo ngữ ('Only at the final stage does the electricity reach ...'), absolute clause ('the output of numerous strings being aggregated') và lexis chính xác hơn ('delineates', 'discrete stages', 'harnessed', 'conveyed', 'elevates').
•  Band 8 điều phối sequencer + bị động liền mạch hơn ('Thereafter ... so that ...'), trong khi Band 7 lặp 'then / Following this / Subsequently' nhiều hơn và cohesion phẳng hơn.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Đọc sơ đồ 30 giây để xác định đây là quy trình tuyến tính có MỘT nhánh phụ (battery storage): tìm hai pha lớn (generation/conditioning vs transmission/distribution) làm 'mỏ neo' cho Overview.
•  Viết Overview bằng 2 ý: (1) quy trình chia hai pha, (2) có bank lưu trữ bù cho nguồn solar gián đoạn — KHÔNG nêu mức điện áp 33 kV/230 kV trong Overview.
•  Mặc định dùng thể bị động ('is converted', 'is aggregated', 'is routed', 'is transmitted') vì sơ đồ kỹ thuật không cần tác nhân.
•  Dùng dải sequencer đa dạng: Initially > then > Following this > Subsequently > Finally — và 'after which / before' để nối các bước trong cùng câu, tránh lặp.
•  Đưa số liệu điện áp (480 V → 33 kV → 230 kV) vào thân bài đúng vị trí; khép mạch bằng câu nhẹ về renewable transition thay vì kết luận chủ quan.
T12 — ENERGY & RESOURCES · Writing Task 2
(1) Đề bài
Đề bài.  Nuclear energy should be expanded globally to address climate change. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
(2) Từ vựng chủ đề (Band 8 topic & argument lexis)

rows: I support a measured expansion of nuclear power, provided strict safeguards apply.
Nuclear's chief advantage is its energy density and round-the-clock reliability.
A single reactor can supply gigawatts of low-carbon baseload power continuously.
It is the dispatchable nature of nuclear that complements intermittent renewables.
sự cố nóng chảy lò phản ứng
Reactor meltdowns at Chernobyl and Fukushima rendered vast areas uninhabitable.
chất thải phóng xạ mức cao
The safe storage of high-level radioactive waste remains an unresolved problem.
Geological disposal of spent fuel is feasible yet politically intractable.
Small modular reactors are factory-built, passively safe and far cheaper.
cơ cấu năng lượng / đa dạng hóa lưới
Pairing reactors with renewables would diversify the grid and stabilise supply.
Neither nuclear nor renewables is a panacea for the climate emergency.

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Phía ủng hộ mở rộng (có kiểm soát):
•  Mật độ năng lượng và độ tin cậy cao: một lò có thể cấp điện nền carbon thấp suốt ngày đêm, không phụ thuộc thời tiết.
•  Bản chất dispatchable bổ trợ cho điện gió/mặt trời gián đoạn — IEA cho rằng khó đạt net-zero nếu thiếu nguồn phát ổn định carbon thấp.
•  Nước bỏ điện hạt nhân sớm (vd Đức) phải đốt thêm than trong giai đoạn chuyển đổi, làm tăng phát thải.
Phía dè dặt (rủi ro & chi phí):
•  Sự cố như Chernobyl/Fukushima cho thấy một tai nạn đơn lẻ có thể khiến cả vùng đất không ở được trong nhiều thế hệ.
•  Lưu trữ chất thải phóng xạ mức cao vẫn là bài toán kỹ thuật-chính trị chưa có lời giải.
•  Chi phí vốn và thời gian xây lò truyền thống cực lớn (hàng chục tỷ USD, kéo dài nhiều thập kỷ).
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — diễn giải đề (mở rộng hạt nhân toàn cầu để chống biến đổi khí hậu); thesis: phần lớn đồng tình với mở rộng CÓ kiểm soát dựa trên thiết kế mới.
•  Body 1 — lập luận ủng hộ: điện nền carbon thấp, dispatchable bổ trợ tái tạo, bằng chứng IEA và bài học Đức bỏ hạt nhân.
•  Body 2 — lập luận dè dặt: rủi ro sự cố, chất thải phóng xạ, chi phí vốn và thời gian xây dựng khổng lồ.
•  Conclusion — đồng tình một phần: mở rộng có chọn lọc với lò mô-đun nhỏ và giám sát chặt, lồng vào lưới giàu năng lượng tái tạo.
(5) Mẫu câu luyện tập (Practice sentences)

rows: Câu luận điểm (thesis) có điều kiện
While the technology is not without its hazards, I largely agree that a measured expansion is justified, provided strict safeguards are in place.
Nêu lập trường + điều kiện 'provided ...' ngay ở thesis.
Câu nhấn mạnh lợi ích bằng cleft
It is precisely this dispatchable nature of nuclear that makes it a useful complement to renewables rather than a competitor.
Dùng cleft 'It is ... that' để nhấn luận điểm.
The International Energy Agency has noted that countries which retired their nuclear fleets prematurely ended up burning more coal during the transition.
Dẫn nguồn cụ thể + mệnh đề quan hệ 'which retired ...'.
Câu phản biện chi phí (đảo ngữ điều kiện)
Were these vulnerabilities ignored, a hasty roll-out could trigger public backlash and stall the broader energy transition.
Đảo ngữ 'Were these ... ignored' thay 'If these were ignored'.
Câu kết tổng hợp cân bằng
Embedding small modular reactors within a grid increasingly dominated by renewables would yield a hybrid system both resilient and decarbonised.
Kết hợp giải pháp cụ thể + lợi ích kép, tránh khẩu hiệu.

blocks.text: (6) Nâng cấp tục ngữ → diễn đạt học thuật

rows: "a technology whose substantial benefits are matched by non-trivial risks"
"no panacea, yet a valuable component of a diversified low-carbon mix"
"a near-zero operational carbon footprint coupled with high power density"
"exposing communities to low-probability but high-consequence accidents"

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~286 words)

The proposal to scale up nuclear power as a remedy for the climate emergency has gained renewed traction among policymakers. While the technology is not without its hazards, I largely agree that a measured expansion is justified, provided strict safeguards are in place.

The strongest argument in favour of nuclear lies in its energy density and reliability. Unlike wind and solar — which remain intermittent and require costly storage — a single reactor can supply gigawatts of low-carbon baseload power around the clock. The International Energy Agency has noted that countries which retired their nuclear fleets prematurely, such as Germany, ended up burning more coal during the transition. It is precisely this dispatchable nature of nuclear that makes it a useful complement to renewables rather than a competitor.

That said, the objections are far from trivial. Reactor meltdowns at Chernobyl and Fukushima have demonstrated how a single accident can render vast tracts of land uninhabitable for generations. Furthermore, the safe storage of high-level radioactive waste remains an unresolved engineering problem, with most spent fuel still sitting in cooling pools awaiting a permanent repository. The capital costs and build times of new reactors are also notoriously prohibitive, often running into tens of billions and decades.

In my opinion, these risks justify caution but not outright rejection. New Generation IV designs, including small modular reactors, are inherently safer and produce less long-lived waste. Pairing such reactors with an expanding share of renewables would diversify the grid and accelerate the phase-out of coal.

In conclusion, although the perils of nuclear power should not be downplayed, its capacity to deliver clean baseload electricity is too valuable to discard, and a carefully regulated expansion appears to be the pragmatic path forward.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~295 words)

The contention that a global build-out of nuclear capacity is indispensable to climate stabilisation has resurfaced with surprising vigour. While I do not endorse it without reservation, I broadly concur that a disciplined expansion — anchored in next-generation designs and rigorous oversight — represents one of the most pragmatic levers available.

A compelling rationale for nuclear lies in its near-zero operational carbon footprint coupled with a power density unmatched by any renewable. Whereas a sprawling solar farm may yield only a few hundred megawatts contingent on insolation, a single large reactor delivers a steady gigawatt regardless of meteorological vagaries. The International Energy Agency's Net Zero roadmap accordingly envisages a doubling of installed nuclear capacity, recognising that decarbonising electricity grids without firm low-carbon generation is mathematically improbable. Especially in regions lacking geothermal or hydroelectric endowment, nuclear may be the only dispatchable substitute for fossil-fired plants.

Detractors, nevertheless, marshal arguments that cannot be dismissed lightly. The legacy of Fukushima continues to haunt public opinion, and the geological disposal of high-level waste remains technically feasible yet politically intractable. Equally troubling are the astronomical capital expenditures and build timelines of conventional reactors, which routinely overrun by a decade. Were these vulnerabilities ignored, a hasty roll-out could trigger backlash and stall the broader energy transition.

The resolution, in my view, lies in selective rather than indiscriminate deployment. Small modular reactors — factory-built, passively safe and an order of magnitude cheaper — promise to mitigate many of these structural drawbacks. Embedding them within a grid increasingly dominated by renewables would yield a hybrid system both resilient and decarbonised.

To sum up, although nuclear power is no panacea and its risks merit sober scrutiny, abandoning it would substantially impair humanity's chances of meeting mid-century climate targets, making prudent expansion the wiser course.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày đặc hơn: đảo ngữ ('Were these vulnerabilities ignored ...', 'Equally troubling are the astronomical capital expenditures ...') và nominalisation ('the geological disposal of high-level waste', 'a doubling of installed nuclear capacity'), trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một cleft.

•  Band 8 nâng lexis lên bậc Band 8 ('operational carbon footprint', 'meteorological vagaries', 'firm low-carbon generation', 'politically intractable', 'an order of magnitude cheaper') và bám sát register chuyển dịch năng lượng (IEA Net Zero roadmap), thay cho cụm hơi đời thường như 'ended up burning' ở Band 7.

•  Band 8 lập luận sắc hơn (đối lập solar 'a few hundred megawatts' với reactor 'a steady gigawatt', kết bằng 'selective rather than indiscriminate deployment') và cohesion mượt hơn ('Whereas ...', 'Detractors, nevertheless ...'), nâng Task Response & Coherence một bậc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Finite nghĩa là hữu hạn, có giới hạn và sẽ cạn kiệt nếu dùng mãi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We will run out of oil soon because it is a **finite** resource that cannot be replenished.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Fin' trong finite giống với 'finish' (kết thúc), giúp nhớ rằng đây là thứ có giới hạn, sẽ đi đến hồi kết.
vocabulary.common_error: Học viên hay nhầm 'finite' với 'infinite' (vô hạn) vì chỉ khác một tiền tố nhưng nghĩa trái ngược hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.definition_en: limited in size or extent; having an end or a fixed quantity rather than being endless
vocabulary.definition_vi: hữu hạn, có giới hạn, không phải là vô tận
vocabulary.example: We will run out of oil soon because it is a finite resource that cannot be replenished.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Fin' giống 'finish' (kết thúc) → 'finite' là thứ có điểm kết thúc, tức là hữu hạn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Intermittent nghĩa là gián đoạn, xảy ra không liên tục mà theo từng đợt ngắt quãng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Renewable sources are often **intermittent**, since the sun doesn't always shine, creating instability for the national grid.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'inter-' (ở giữa) với ý 'ngắt' để nhớ đây là hiện tượng bị đứt quãng giữa chừng, không liên tục.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'intermittent' (ngắt quãng, có tính chu kỳ) với 'temporary' (tạm thời, ngắn hạn) - hai từ mang sắc thái khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: occurring at irregular intervals; not continuous or steady
vocabulary.definition_vi: gián đoạn, không liên tục, xảy ra ngắt quãng
vocabulary.example: Renewable sources are often intermittent, since the sun doesn't always shine, creating instability for the national grid.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Inter-' (giữa) + 'mit' (gửi/ngắt) → tín hiệu bị ngắt quãng giữa chừng, không liên tục.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Renewable nghĩa là có thể tái tạo được một cách tự nhiên, không bị cạn kiệt khi sử dụng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Solar power is a clean and **renewable** energy source that does not harm the earth.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Re-' (lại) cộng 'new' (mới) giúp nhớ đây là nguồn năng lượng liên tục được làm mới, không cạn kiệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Tránh nhầm 'renewable' (tái tạo được) với 'reusable' (tái sử dụng được) - hai khái niệm áp dụng cho tài nguyên khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of an energy source) able to be replenished naturally and not depleted when used
vocabulary.definition_vi: tái tạo được, không bị cạn kiệt khi sử dụng
vocabulary.example: Solar power is a clean and renewable energy source that does not harm the earth.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Re-' (lại) + 'new' (mới) → nguồn năng lượng luôn được làm mới lại, không bao giờ cạn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Harness nghĩa là khai thác và kiểm soát một nguồn lực tự nhiên để phục vụ mục đích thực tế.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Technologies that **harness** solar, wind and hydroelectric power are becoming increasingly efficient.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng đến bộ yên cương (harness) buộc vào ngựa để điều khiển sức mạnh của nó, giống như việc khai thác năng lượng tự nhiên.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Harness' mang nghĩa tích cực (khai thác một cách có kiểm soát), khác với 'exploit' vốn có thể mang sắc thái tiêu cực (bóc lột).
vocabulary.definition_en: to capture and control the power of something, especially a natural force, and use it for a practical purpose
vocabulary.definition_vi: khai thác và sử dụng (một nguồn lực tự nhiên) cho mục đích thực tế
vocabulary.example: Technologies that harness solar, wind and hydroelectric power are becoming increasingly efficient.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung bộ 'yên cương' (harness) buộc vào ngựa để điều khiển sức mạnh của nó - tương tự như khai thác năng lượng tự nhiên.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Radioactive nghĩa là có tính phóng xạ, tức là phát ra bức xạ ion hóa nguy hiểm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Nuclear waste remains highly **radioactive** and dangerous for thousands of years.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'radio' (bức xạ) với 'active' (đang hoạt động) để nhớ nghĩa là đang chủ động phát ra bức xạ.
vocabulary.common_error: Danh từ tương ứng là 'radioactivity' (tính phóng xạ), không phải 'radioactiveness' - lỗi thường gặp khi danh từ hóa.
vocabulary.definition_en: emitting or relating to the emission of ionising radiation or particles
vocabulary.definition_vi: có tính phóng xạ, phát ra bức xạ ion hóa
vocabulary.example: Nuclear waste remains highly radioactive and dangerous for thousands of years.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Radio' (bức xạ) + 'active' (hoạt động) → vật chất đang chủ động phát ra bức xạ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Geothermal nghĩa là địa nhiệt, tức là liên quan đến nhiệt lượng sinh ra từ bên trong lòng đất.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Countries like Iceland have successfully utilised **geothermal** energy to power entire cities.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'geo' (trái đất) với 'thermal' (nhiệt) để nhớ đây là năng lượng nhiệt lấy từ lòng đất.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Geothermal' là tính từ, không dùng làm danh từ độc lập - phải đi kèm danh từ như 'geothermal energy/power'.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to or produced by the internal heat of the earth
vocabulary.definition_vi: địa nhiệt, liên quan đến nhiệt lượng bên trong lòng đất
vocabulary.example: Countries like Iceland have successfully utilised geothermal energy to power entire cities.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Geo' (trái đất) + 'thermal' (nhiệt) → năng lượng nhiệt lấy từ lòng đất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Combustion nghĩa là sự đốt cháy nhiên liệu để tạo ra nhiệt và ánh sáng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> For over a century, industrial development has been powered by the **combustion** of fossil fuels.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Âm 'bust' trong combustion gợi liên tưởng đến lửa bùng lên khi nhiên liệu bị đốt cháy.
vocabulary.common_error: Tính từ 'combustible' (dễ cháy) khác với 'combustive' - dạng sau không tồn tại trong tiếng Anh chuẩn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of burning a fuel to produce heat and light
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự đốt cháy, quá trình đốt nhiên liệu để tạo nhiệt và ánh sáng
vocabulary.example: For over a century, industrial development has been powered by the combustion of fossil fuels.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Combust' nghe gần giống 'bust' (nổ, bùng) → hình dung lửa bùng lên khi đốt cháy nhiên liệu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Consumption nghĩa là sự tiêu thụ, tức là việc sử dụng nhiên liệu, năng lượng hoặc tài nguyên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We use too much electricity in our daily lives, and curbing this high **consumption** has become an urgent priority.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Consume' nghĩa là tiêu thụ hết, nên 'consumption' là hành động liên tục sử dụng và tiêu hao năng lượng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Consumption' (sự tiêu thụ) khác với 'consumerism' (chủ nghĩa tiêu dùng) - không dùng thay thế cho nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: the use of something, especially fuel, energy, or natural resources
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tiêu thụ, việc sử dụng năng lượng hoặc tài nguyên thiên nhiên
vocabulary.example: We use too much electricity in our daily lives, and curbing this high consumption has become an urgent priority.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Consume' nghĩa là 'tiêu thụ, ăn hết' → 'consumption' là hành động tiêu thụ liên tục năng lượng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sustainability nghĩa là tính bền vững, khả năng duy trì lâu dài mà không làm cạn kiệt tài nguyên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The ultimate goal is to achieve long-term environmental **sustainability** across every sector of the economy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Sustain' nghĩa là duy trì, nên 'sustainability' là khả năng duy trì được lâu dài, tức là tính bền vững.
vocabulary.common_error: Học viên hay viết sai chính tả thành 'sustainbility', thiếu âm tiết 'a' trước 'bility'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the ability to be maintained at a certain level over the long term without depleting resources or causing lasting harm
vocabulary.definition_vi: tính bền vững, khả năng duy trì lâu dài mà không làm cạn kiệt tài nguyên
vocabulary.example: The ultimate goal is to achieve long-term environmental sustainability across every sector of the economy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Sustain' nghĩa là 'duy trì' → 'sustainability' là khả năng duy trì được lâu dài, bền vững.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Grid nghĩa là lưới điện, tức là mạng lưới phân phối điện năng trong một khu vực hoặc quốc gia.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Renewable sources are often intermittent, creating instability for the national **grid**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung lưới điện như một tấm lưới ô vuông giăng khắp đất nước, kết nối mọi nơi với nhau.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Grid' luôn viết thường trong ngữ cảnh chung; chỉ viết hoa 'National Grid' khi nói đến tên riêng công ty lưới điện của Anh.
vocabulary.definition_en: a network of cables or pipes for distributing power, especially electricity, throughout a region or country
vocabulary.definition_vi: lưới điện, mạng lưới phân phối điện năng trong một khu vực hoặc quốc gia
vocabulary.example: Renewable sources are often intermittent, creating instability for the national grid.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung lưới điện như một tấm lưới ô vuông (grid) giăng khắp cả nước, kết nối mọi nơi với nhau.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Decommission nghĩa là ngừng vận hành vĩnh viễn một nhà máy hoặc hệ thống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many developed nations are planning to **decommission** coal plants entirely as part of their net-zero pledges.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'De-' (ngược lại) cộng 'commission' (đưa vào hoạt động) tạo thành hành động ngừng hẳn hoạt động của một nhà máy.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Decommission' (ngừng vận hành vĩnh viễn) khác với 'shut down' tạm thời (có thể mở lại) - decommission thường mang tính dứt điểm, lâu dài.
vocabulary.definition_en: to take (a plant, machine, or system) out of active service permanently
vocabulary.definition_vi: ngừng vận hành vĩnh viễn (một nhà máy hoặc hệ thống)
vocabulary.example: Many developed nations are planning to decommission coal plants entirely as part of their net-zero pledges.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'De-' (ngược lại) + 'commission' (đưa vào hoạt động) → làm ngược lại việc đưa vào hoạt động, tức là ngừng hẳn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Self-sufficient nghĩa là tự cung tự cấp, có thể đáp ứng nhu cầu của mình mà không cần dựa vào bên ngoài.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Our rooftop solar array generates the bulk of our daytime electricity, making the household almost energy **self-sufficient**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'self' (tự thân) với 'sufficient' (đủ) để nhớ nghĩa là tự bản thân đã đủ, không cần nhờ vào bên ngoài.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn viết có dấu gạch nối 'self-sufficient', không viết rời thành hai từ 'self sufficient'.
vocabulary.definition_en: able to provide for one's own needs without external help, especially in terms of resources or energy
vocabulary.definition_vi: tự cung tự cấp, không cần dựa vào bên ngoài
vocabulary.example: Our rooftop solar array generates the bulk of our daytime electricity, making the household almost energy self-sufficient.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Self' (tự thân) + 'sufficient' (đủ) → tự bản thân đã đủ, không cần nhờ bên ngoài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Nuclear nghĩa là hạt nhân, liên quan đến năng lượng sinh ra từ phản ứng hạt nhân của nguyên tử.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A single reactor can supply gigawatts of low-carbon baseload power through **nuclear** power generation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng đến 'nucleus' (nhân nguyên tử) để nhớ rằng 'nuclear' là năng lượng lấy từ chính hạt nhân nguyên tử.
vocabulary.common_error: Phát âm dễ sai thành 'nu-cu-lar' - trọng âm và thứ tự âm tiết đúng là /ˈnjuː.kli.ə/.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to the energy released by reactions involving the nucleus of an atom, especially fission
vocabulary.definition_vi: hạt nhân, liên quan đến năng lượng sinh ra từ phản ứng hạt nhân
vocabulary.example: A single reactor can supply gigawatts of low-carbon baseload power through nuclear power generation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng đến 'nucleus' (nhân tế bào/nguyên tử) - 'nuclear' là năng lượng lấy từ chính hạt nhân nguyên tử.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Come under scrutiny nghĩa là bị đưa ra xem xét, giám sát một cách chặt chẽ và kỹ lưỡng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The aviation industry has **come under** intense scrutiny for its significant contribution to global carbon emissions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung một vật bị đặt dưới kính lúp để soi xét kỹ từng chi tiết, giống như bị giám sát chặt chẽ.
vocabulary.common_error: Sau 'come under' luôn dùng danh từ 'scrutiny', không chia thành động từ 'scrutinise' trong cụm này.
vocabulary.definition_en: to start being examined or investigated very closely and critically
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị đưa ra xem xét, giám sát chặt chẽ
vocabulary.example: The aviation industry has come under intense scrutiny for its significant contribution to global carbon emissions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một vật bị đặt dưới kính lúp (scrutiny) để soi xét từng chi tiết một cách chặt chẽ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Grapple with nghĩa là vật lộn, cố gắng hết sức để giải quyết một vấn đề khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Policymakers must **grapple with** the immense challenge of phasing out fossil fuels without triggering an economic collapse.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung hai đô vật đang ôm vật lộn với nhau, giống như việc phải cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề nan giải.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn đi kèm giới từ 'with' sau 'grapple' - không dùng 'grapple a problem' thiếu giới từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem or challenge
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn, cố gắng giải quyết một vấn đề khó khăn
vocabulary.example: Policymakers must grapple with the immense challenge of phasing out fossil fuels without triggering an economic collapse.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung hai đô vật ôm vật lộn (grapple) với nhau, giống như việc phải vật lộn để giải quyết một vấn đề khó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
A contentious issue nghĩa là một vấn đề gây tranh cãi, gây bất đồng quan điểm sâu sắc giữa các bên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Whether to expand nuclear capacity remains **a contentious issue**, dividing environmentalists who see it as essential and those who fear its risks.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Contend' nghĩa là tranh luận, đấu tranh, nên 'a contentious issue' là một vấn đề khiến người ta phải tranh luận gay gắt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Contentious' (gây tranh cãi) dễ bị nhầm với 'contentious' phát âm sai thành 'con-TEN-shus' đọc nhanh mất âm; trọng âm đúng rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai.
vocabulary.definition_en: a topic that causes strong disagreement or heated debate between different groups
vocabulary.definition_vi: một vấn đề gây tranh cãi, gây bất đồng quan điểm sâu sắc
vocabulary.example: Whether to expand nuclear capacity remains a contentious issue, dividing environmentalists who see it as essential and those who fear its risks.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Contend' (tranh luận, đấu tranh) + '-ious' → một vấn đề khiến người ta phải 'tranh luận' gay gắt với nhau.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Dispatchable nghĩa là có thể phát điện theo nhu cầu, chủ động bật hoặc điều chỉnh khi cần.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Coal and gas plants offer **dispatchable** power, while solar and wind, by contrast, are intermittent.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Dispatch' nghĩa là điều động ngay lập tức, nên 'dispatchable' là nguồn điện có thể được điều động bật lên bất cứ khi nào cần.
vocabulary.common_error: Trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai (dis-PATCH-a-ble), không phải âm đầu - lỗi phát âm phổ biến.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a power source) able to be turned on or off, or adjusted in output, on demand to meet grid needs
vocabulary.definition_vi: có thể phát điện theo nhu cầu, chủ động điều chỉnh được
vocabulary.example: Coal and gas plants offer dispatchable power, while solar and wind, by contrast, are intermittent.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Dispatch' nghĩa là 'điều động, gửi đi ngay' → nguồn điện có thể được 'điều động' bật lên bất cứ khi nào cần.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Baseload nghĩa là điện nền, tức là mức phát điện tối thiểu phải duy trì liên tục suốt ngày đêm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Nuclear energy provides a massive, reliable **baseload**, unlike solar and wind which depend on the weather.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ghép 'base' (nền tảng) với 'load' (tải) để nhớ đây là mức tải điện nền luôn phải duy trì liên tục.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Baseload' là danh từ ghép chỉ mức tải nền tối thiểu, không nhầm với 'workload' (khối lượng công việc).
vocabulary.definition_en: the minimum continuous level of electricity demand or supply that a grid must meet around the clock
vocabulary.definition_vi: điện nền, mức phát điện tối thiểu và liên tục suốt ngày đêm
vocabulary.example: Nuclear energy provides a massive, reliable baseload, unlike solar and wind which depend on the weather.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Base' (nền tảng) + 'load' (tải) → mức tải điện nền tảng luôn phải duy trì liên tục.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Decarbonisation nghĩa là quá trình khử carbon, tức là giảm dần hoặc loại bỏ phát thải khí CO2.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Decarbonisation** is not a technical problem; it is a stranded-asset problem, as trillions of dollars of coal mines and pipelines must be written off.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'De-' (loại bỏ) cộng 'carbon' giúp nhớ đây là quá trình loại bỏ dần lượng khí carbon thải ra môi trường.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả Anh-Anh 'decarbonisation' (-isation), không viết kiểu Mỹ 'decarbonization' (-ization).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions from an activity, sector, or economy
vocabulary.definition_vi: quá trình khử carbon, giảm phát thải khí CO2
vocabulary.example: Decarbonisation is not a technical problem; it is a stranded-asset problem, as trillions of dollars of coal mines and pipelines must be written off.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'De-' (loại bỏ) + 'carbon' (carbon) → quá trình loại bỏ dần lượng carbon thải ra.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Stranded asset nghĩa là tài sản mắc kẹt, mất giá trị sớm trước khi hết vòng đời sử dụng dự kiến.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Trillions of dollars of coal mines, refineries and pipelines must be written off as **stranded assets** during the energy transition.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'Stranded' nghĩa là mắc cạn, giống như con tàu mắc cạn không đi tiếp được, tài sản này cũng vậy - mất giá trị và bị bỏ lại.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ khác (ví dụ 'stranded-asset problem'), cần thêm dấu gạch nối.
vocabulary.definition_en: an investment or resource that has lost its value or become a liability before the end of its expected useful life, often due to policy or market shifts
vocabulary.definition_vi: tài sản mắc kẹt, khoản đầu tư mất giá trị sớm do thay đổi chính sách hoặc thị trường
vocabulary.example: Trillions of dollars of coal mines, refineries and pipelines must be written off as stranded assets during the energy transition.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'Stranded' nghĩa là 'mắc cạn' (như tàu mắc cạn) → tài sản 'mắc cạn', không còn dùng được nữa.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Run out of steam nghĩa là hụt hơi, mất đà và không thể tiếp tục với cùng tốc độ như ban đầu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The environmental campaign started well but quickly **ran out of steam** halfway through.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Liên tưởng đầu máy hơi nước hết hơi sẽ dừng lại, giống như một dự án cạn nhiệt huyết giữa chừng.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là thành ngữ cố định, không chia động từ 'run' thành các dạng khác trong cụm cố định 'run out of steam'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to gradually lose energy, momentum, or enthusiasm and be unable to continue at the same pace
vocabulary.definition_vi: hụt hơi, mất đà, cạn nhiệt huyết giữa chừng
vocabulary.example: The environmental campaign started well but quickly ran out of steam halfway through.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Liên tưởng đầu máy hơi nước (steam engine) hết hơi nước sẽ dừng lại - giống như một dự án cạn nhiệt huyết giữa chừng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Recharge one's batteries nghĩa là nghỉ ngơi để nạp lại năng lượng và nhiệt huyết.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After finishing this exhausting project, I really need a holiday to **recharge my batteries**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung bản thân như một cục pin cần được sạc lại sau một quãng thời gian làm việc mệt mỏi.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn chia sở hữu cách phù hợp chủ ngữ (my/your/his batteries), không dùng 'the batteries' chung chung trong idiom này.
vocabulary.definition_en: to rest and relax in order to restore one's energy and enthusiasm
vocabulary.definition_vi: nạp lại năng lượng, nghỉ ngơi để lấy lại sức
vocabulary.example: After finishing this exhausting project, I really need a holiday to recharge my batteries.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung bản thân như một cục pin (battery) cần được sạc lại (recharge) sau khi làm việc mệt mỏi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Burn the candle at both ends nghĩa là làm việc quá sức, thức khuya dậy sớm không còn thời gian nghỉ ngơi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> You look completely exhausted; you need to stop **burning the candle at both ends**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình dung một cây nến bị đốt ở cả hai đầu cùng lúc sẽ cháy hết rất nhanh, giống như một người làm việc kiệt sức.
collocations: stop burning the candle at both ends
burning the candle at both ends for weeks
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là idiom nguyên khối, không đảo trật tự hay bỏ từ 'both' - phải giữ đúng 'at both ends'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to work or engage in activities from early morning until late at night, leaving too little time for rest
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm việc quá sức, thức khuya dậy sớm không có thời gian nghỉ ngơi
vocabulary.example: You look completely exhausted; you need to stop burning the candle at both ends.
vocabulary.headword: Burn the candle at both ends
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình dung một cây nến bị đốt ở cả hai đầu cùng lúc, sẽ cháy hết rất nhanh - giống như một người làm việc kiệt sức.
vocabulary.syllables: burn the CAN-dle at BOTH ends

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Go green nghĩa là chuyển sang lối sống hoặc hoạt động thân thiện hơn với môi trường.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many corporations are deciding to **go green** to attract more environmentally conscious customers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Màu xanh lá tượng trưng cho thiên nhiên, nên 'go green' là đi theo hướng thân thiện với môi trường.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Go green' là cụm cố định không chia thời quá khứ thành 'went green' khi mô tả xu hướng chung, chỉ dùng khi kể việc cụ thể đã hoàn thành.
vocabulary.definition_en: to adopt more environmentally friendly practices, especially by reducing pollution or using sustainable resources
vocabulary.definition_vi: chuyển sang lối sống/hoạt động thân thiện với môi trường
vocabulary.example: Many corporations are deciding to go green to attract more environmentally conscious customers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Màu xanh lá (green) tượng trưng cho thiên nhiên - 'go green' là 'đi theo màu xanh', tức là sống thân thiện với môi trường.
